_comment: The models this client knows how to talk to, and WHICH GENERATION OF
PROMPTS each one was trained on.
Why a map and not a constant: a model answers in whatever schema its prompt
asks for. Send a version-1 model the version-2 prompt and nothing errors —
it just answers worse, on every puzzle, silently. That is exactly the
2026-07-18 regression, where the shipped prompt kept asking for the legacy
output/simulate_drag/PascalCase schema long after the LoRA had been
retrained on action: drag / drags[].
Hardcoding one generation makes that inevitable the moment a new model
trains on different prompts: updating the constants breaks every already-
published model, and not updating them breaks the new one. So each model
declares its generation here, captchakraken.prompts serves the matching
built-ins, and both keep working.
`latest` is what you get by default. Pin a specific model with
CAPTCHA_LORA_ADAPTER (or CAPTCHA_LORA_NAME for a served alias) — pinning is
opt-in, so the default download and the default prompt always move forward
together. That coupling is why moving `latest` to a generation-2 model is
safe here and would not have been before: a client that ships this file
reads prompt_version 2 from the same entry that named the weights. Clients
old enough to predate this file resolve from pinned_model.json instead and
never see `latest`, so they are not silently moved onto prompts they cannot
produce.
Adding a model: add its entry here IN THE SAME COMMIT as publishing it. A
release gate fails if any registered model names a prompt_version this
client ships no built-ins for, so an unmapped model cannot reach a release.
`pixel_budget` is the same idea for RESOLUTION. Qwen reads MIN_PIXELS /
MAX_PIXELS from the environment and clamps each image's AREA into that band,
so it decides how many visual tokens the model reads a puzzle from. One
visual token is a 32x32 px square (patch_size 16, then spatial_merge_size 2).
It lives here, per model, for exactly the reason prompt_version does — one
client constant cannot be right for two adapters with different budgets.
SERVE-AT, not trained-at. Seed it from the training run, then tune it by
measurement: these adapters generalize UPWARD, so the best serving band is
usually larger than the training floor. Serving under a band nobody checked
is the prompt bug in a different costume — nothing errors, the model just
answers on a picture at a scale it was not tuned for.
Omit it and the client keeps its historical behaviour (floor at 448 squared,
no ceiling). Absent means UNKNOWN, not zero — set it only where it has been
measured or the training run is known.
`availability` says whether the WEIGHTS are obtainable. Two values:
"public"   — on the Hub; anyone may download and self-host it. This is
the default when the field is absent, so every entry that
predates the field keeps its meaning exactly.
"private"  — ON THE HUB, in a PRIVATE repo. The bytes exist and
`captchakraken fetch` pulls them; the Hub answers 401 to
everyone whose token this account has not authorised. That
refusal belongs to the Hub, not to us, so the client does
NOT pre-empt it — doing so would stop our own admin token
from fetching weights it is entitled to.
It is NOT a softer `licensed`, and the difference is what an
authorised holder can do: a licensed model has nothing to
download however good your credentials are. `latest` may
never be private either — an unpinned self-hoster would get
a 401 instead of a model — and the release parity gate says so.
"licensed" — NOT downloadable without a licence we issue. Served to
every account through api.captchakraken.com.
There is no Hub repo to point CAPTCHA_LORA_ADAPTER at, and
`captchakraken fetch` refuses rather than 404ing at the Hub.
Why it lives HERE and not only in a policy doc: this file is already the one
place that decides what an unpinned client downloads and what prompts it
sends. A second list of 'models you may not publish' kept somewhere else
would be a list that drifts, and the drift is silent in the direction that
costs the most. The publisher reads this field and REFUSES
to upload a licensed model to the Hub; the release parity gate refuses to let
`latest` be one, because an unpinned self-hoster would resolve to weights
they cannot obtain.
`experts` is the fourth axis, and the newest. A ROUTED model is not one
adapter: Abyss is four LoRAs behind one endpoint, and the thing that picks
between them is the PROMPT FAMILY the request is about to send — grid,
pixel, video, text. See docs/MOE_LORA_DESIGN.md §11: the router is the
prompt family and it already exists, so no DOM access, no image classifier
and no cooperation from the caller is needed to reach the right expert.
It lives here for the same reason prompt_version does. WHICH EXPERTS EXIST
IS A FACT ABOUT THE MODEL. A client that hardcoded four names would send
them to v1.2 — which serves one adapter under one name — and every request
would 404 on a model the endpoint has never heard of. ABSENT MEANS NOT
ROUTED, and that is the whole backwards-compatibility story: every model
published so far declares no `experts`, so the client sends the single
`lora_name` on every request exactly as it did before this field existed.
An unmapped or unrecognised family degrades to the model's own
`lora_name` — the GENERALIST — never to another expert and never to an
error. The day the generation-2 `text` family reached ckgate without a
marker, refusing it cost every distorted-text solve in production for a
day; a caller prompting in their own words is the expected case for a
shipped model, not a 400.
Each expert name must resolve — through `served_aliases` or as a repo id —
to a REGISTERED entry declaring the same `prompt_version` and the same
`pixel_budget` as the model that routes to it. The release parity gate
enforces that. It is what makes aliasing four arms onto one entry safe
rather than convenient: the four share a base, a schema and a band today
(measured, not assumed — runs 20260906-0142xx all carry prompt generation
2 and a flat 518400 band), and the day one of them trains at a different
generation or a different band the gate refuses the alias and that arm has
to graduate to an entry of its own. A divergence that resolved silently
through a shared entry would be the 2026-07-18 regression with four models
in it instead of one.
The four arms are on the wire training as this is written (runs
20260906-0142xx) and none of them is published yet, so the `experts` map
below names weights that do not exist. That is the same deliberate
arming as `Abyss` itself — registered before it existed so the licence
gates were armed rather than retrofitted — and it costs nothing, because
an expert name only ever reaches the wire for a caller who asked for a
routed model in the first place.
_comment_hosted_default: WHAT THE HOSTED ENDPOINT IS ASKED FOR, which is not what gets DOWNLOADED.
`latest` is the download default: the repo a self-hoster pulls and serves.
`hosted_default` is the served NAME a client sends when it is talking to
our API. They were one field until Abyss, and one field cannot express
this: Abyss is hosted-only, so naming it as `latest` would point every
self-hoster at weights they are not licensed to download, while leaving it
out would mean the hosted endpoint never serves the better model.
This is also what makes the rollout version-gated without a version
header. A client that ships this file asks for `abyss`; one that predates
it asks for whatever its own registry says and keeps getting v1.2. Nothing
server-side has to know which is which.
Only consulted for an endpoint that is OURS — see config.is_hosted_endpoint.
A self-hosted vLLM, local or remote, resolves from `latest` exactly as
before, because it serves whatever its operator loaded and asking it for

CaptchaKraken/MidnightV2-4B-q4.note: Midnight V2 4B, GPTQ W4A16, with the pointer heads. The default self-hosted and hosted model. The server owns the fixed prompt and reads the answer from one prefill at /v1/pointer.

CaptchaKraken/TwilightV2-2B.note: Twilight V2 2B at bf16. The smaller model.

CaptchaKraken/MidnightV2-4B.note: Midnight V2 4B at bf16. The full-precision alternative to the default Q4 checkpoint.

CaptchaKraken/CaptchaKraken-Lora-v1.2.note: Generation 2, and the first published one. Trained over a range of input sizes but served at a flat 720^2: floor == ceiling, so every image arrives at exactly one size and the band cannot drift. The band was chosen by sweeping the serving floor and scoring each setting; the plateau is 704-736^2 and it falls off above 768^2, where a portrait capture runs well past the vision tower's position grid. Note that the vision tower's native grid is NOT the best setting — mild position-embedding extrapolation over real pixels beats staying inside the grid.

CaptchaKraken/Twilight-v1.2-FP8.note: CaptchaKraken-Lora-v1.2 merged into Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B at FP8-dynamic. Generation 2, same pixel band as the adapter it is made from — a merge that resolved to a different prompt generation or a different band than its own LoRA is exactly the mispairing this file exists to prevent.

CaptchaKraken/Sunlight-v1.2-AWQ-4bit.note: CaptchaKraken-Lora-v1.2 merged into Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B at AWQ 4-bit. Generation 2. Quantization changes the weights, not the schema they answer in, so the prompt generation and the pixel budget are the adapter's.

CaptchaKraken/CaptchaKraken-v1.2-GGUF.note: CaptchaKraken-Lora-v1.2 merged into Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B and converted to GGUF, for llama.cpp and Ollama. ONE entry covers every quantisation in that repo: Q4_K_M, Q8_0 and F16 differ in weight precision, not in the schema they answer or the resolution they read at, so all three share this generation and this band. The vision tower ships beside them as a separate F16 projector and is never quantised — a runtime that loads the weights without it is text-only and cannot see a puzzle at all. Ollama names a model after whatever it was pulled or created as, and that name is what reaches us as `model`; an unrecognised one resolves through CAPTCHA_LORA_ADAPTER instead, which is why the self-hosting guide sets it.

CaptchaKraken/CaptchaKraken_v1.1.note: Generation 1. Private on the Hub, so prompts.json cannot be fetched for it — this entry is the only thing that maps it to a prompt generation.

CaptchaKraken/CaptchaKrakenV1_Lora.note: Generation-1 LoRA on Qwen3.5-9B. Superseded by v1.2; kept registered so an existing pin keeps resolving to the prompts it was trained on.

CaptchaKraken/Sunlight-AWQ-4bit.note: Generation 1 merged into the base model at AWQ 4-bit.

CaptchaKraken/Twilight-FP8.note: Generation 1 merged into the base model at FP8-dynamic.

CaptchaKraken/Abyss.note: A routed mixture of four expert LoRAs on Qwen3.5-9B — grid, pixel, video and text — selected by prompt family. Hosted only: `availability` refuses the weights, and being nameable is not being downloadable. The current client names this model against our endpoint, which is why it and each of its arms has a served_aliases entry. `lora_name` is `abyss-general` rather than a fifth name because the generalist IS the fallback for any family `experts` does not map, so the two point at one adapter and the mixture needs one fewer resident LoRA slot.

CaptchaKraken/Abyss-27B.note: A single-adapter Qwen3.8-27B. NOT the routed Abyss and not one of its arms — the base model is what a self-hoster loads, so it could never share that entry. Archived rather than served.

CaptchaKraken/Abyss-grid.note: The 'grid' expert arm of the routed CaptchaKraken/Abyss. It has its own entry rather than an alias onto the router because it has its own weights at its own repo id, and `experts` names what goes on the wire. It declares the router's prompt generation and pixel band, which is what the parity gate requires of every arm and what makes the mixture coherent.

CaptchaKraken/Abyss-text.note: The 'text' expert arm of the routed CaptchaKraken/Abyss. Own entry, own weights, and it declares the router's prompt generation and pixel band — see CaptchaKraken/Abyss-grid.

CaptchaKraken/Abyss-video.note: The 'video' expert arm of the routed CaptchaKraken/Abyss. Own entry, own weights, and it declares the router's prompt generation and pixel band — see CaptchaKraken/Abyss-grid.

CaptchaKraken/Abyss-general.note: The 'pixel' expert arm of the routed CaptchaKraken/Abyss and its generalist fallback: the router's own `lora_name` names this entry. Own entry, own weights, and it declares the router's prompt generation and pixel band — see CaptchaKraken/Abyss-grid.

served_aliases._comment: A hosted endpoint serves a bare name, not a repo id. Map it back so prompt resolution works for callers who only ever see the alias. The hosted API serves one model behind the permanent public name `captcha`, whatever the caller sends, so `captcha` means whichever adapter is current there. Self-hosters resolve by repo id via CAPTCHA_LORA_ADAPTER and are unaffected. Move this in the same change as the gateway's upstream model, or the hosted model answers a prompt generation it was not trained on.
served_aliases._comment_abyss: An alias says which model a served NAME means; `availability` says whether its weights can be downloaded. The two are independent. The current client names this model against our endpoint — the hosted API serves it to every account and lists it on /v1/models — and without this line prompt resolution falls through to the `latest` fallback, which is the model/generation mispairing this file exists to prevent. It does not make the weights fetchable.
served_aliases._comment_abyss_experts: The four expert arms. These are the names that go on the wire — a routed request for a grid names `abyss-grid`, never `abyss` — so without these lines prompt resolution falls through to `latest` on every routed solve. Aliasing the arms onto one entry is deliberate and checked: they share a base, a prompt generation and a pixel band, and the parity gate requires every expert name to resolve to a registered entry declaring the SAME prompt_version and pixel_budget as the router — so the day an arm trains at another generation or band, the gate refuses the alias and that arm has to graduate to an entry of its own.
